title: Entanglement-assisted continuous-variable concatenated codes for encoding qubits or oscillators
summary: Entanglement-assisted (EA) stabilizer codes enhance the rate of error correction in relation to codes with no pre-shared entanglement. Meanwhile, bosonic error-correcting codes, such as the Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) code, can be concatenated with qubit stabilizer codes to significantly reduce the logical failure probability of those stabilizer codes. First, we combine the above two concepts to propose an EA version of the qubit-into-oscillators concatenated code that chains an EA-stabilizer (outer) code with a GKP (inner) code. As an example we present a three-qubit EA-repetition concatenated with a GKP code. Second, we propose an EA version of the non-Gaussian oscillator-into-oscillators concatenated code that chains a GKP (outer) code with an EA-stabilizer (inner) code. As an example we present a GKP code concatenated with a three-qubit EA repetition code that uses two maximally entangled modes (emodes) and suppresses the variances of both position and momentum quadrature errors of a data mode. Furthermore, we generalize the latter example to a family of GKP code concatenated with a $n$-qubit EA repetition code that uses ${n-1}$ emodes and suppresses the variances of both position and momentum quadrature errors of a data mode by a factor ${1/n}$.
commentary: This research represents a significant advance in quantum error correction by cleverly combining two powerful concepts: entanglement-assisted codes that leverage pre-shared quantum entanglement to boost error correction rates, and concatenated coding schemes that chain different types of codes together for enhanced performance. The work bridges discrete qubit systems with continuous-variable quantum systems using Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill codes, creating hybrid architectures that could be particularly valuable for photonic quantum computers and trapped-ion systems operating in continuous regimes. What makes this especially promising is the demonstrated ability to suppress both position and momentum errors simultaneously while using fewer physical resources than traditional approaches, potentially offering a more efficient path to fault-tolerant quantum computing. The mathematical framework developed here opens new possibilities for tailoring error correction strategies to the specific noise characteristics of different quantum hardware platforms.

title: How to Benchmark Logical Qubit Claims
summary: Insider Brief As the quantum computing sector has evolved, so has the way performance is measured. Early on, qubit count — the number of quantum bits in a processor — was viewed as a key benchmark. Today, researchers increasingly argue that raw qubit count matters less than the number of logical qubits, which can reliably […]
commentary: This article tackles a crucial shift happening in quantum computing evaluation as the field matures beyond simple qubit counting. As companies race to demonstrate fault-tolerant quantum computers, the focus is rightfully moving from raw physical qubits to logical qubits that can actually perform error-corrected computation reliably. The challenge lies in establishing standardized benchmarks for logical qubit performance, since different approaches to quantum error correction make direct comparisons between systems increasingly complex. This shift in measurement philosophy reflects the quantum industry's transition from proof-of-concept demonstrations to building machines that can solve real-world problems.

title: Range-controlled entanglement in Lindbladian skin states of monitored fermions
summary: Reservoir engineering can stabilize states inaccessible to unitary dynamics. Directed particle-conserving dissipation creates Lindbladian skin states, where Pauli exclusion turns edge accumulation into a many-body density imbalance. In a monitored fermion chain with tunable hopping range, we identify, within a Gaussian trajectory approximation, two finite-size scaling regimes: short-range hopping is consistent with complete skin accumulation and area-law entanglement, whereas sufficiently long-range hopping produces a finite bulk tail and effective algebraic sub-volume-law entanglement. Dissipation and coherent hopping thus jointly control skin localization and quantum entanglement, highlighting their close interconnection.
commentary: This article reveals a fascinating connection between quantum dissipation and entanglement that could reshape how we think about controlling quantum states. The researchers show that by carefully tuning how far quantum particles can "hop" in a dissipative system, they can dial the entanglement from simple area-law scaling to more complex sub-volume-law behavior—essentially discovering a new knob for quantum state engineering. This work bridges two major areas of quantum physics: non-Hermitian quantum mechanics (where energy isn't conserved) and quantum many-body systems, potentially opening new pathways for creating exotic quantum states that are impossible with standard unitary evolution. The ability to precisely control entanglement through dissipation could prove valuable for quantum error correction schemes and novel quantum algorithms that harness non-equilibrium dynamics.

title: Satellite-Based Quantum Communication: Performance Evaluation of Discrete-Variable Quantum Key Distribution Protocols
summary: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) has emerged as a fundamentally secure approach to communication in the era of quantum computing, offering protection against threats posed to classical cryptographic schemes such as RSA and Diffie-Hellman. This thesis presents a comprehensive performance analysis of satellite-based QKD protocols, focusing on both prepare-and-measure and entanglement-based schemes under realistic atmospheric and operational conditions. The study begins by introducing the theoretical foundations of quantum communication, including qubits, entanglement, and quantum entropy, and motivates the need for satellite-based QKD to overcome the distance limitations of fiber-based systems. Subsequently, the thesis evaluates four prominent QKD protocols-BB84, B92, BBM92, and E91-using a circular beam propagation model that incorporates atmospheric effects such as diffraction, turbulence, attenuation, and pointing errors, along with environmental noise contributions for uplink and downlink. Comparative numerical simulations reveal that protocol performance is strongly influenced by channel asymmetries, beam propagation characteristics, and noise, providing guidance on optimal protocol selection for low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite links. The research further investigates high-dimensional (HD) QKD protocols, specifically HD-BB84 and HD-Extended B92, using the elliptic-beam approximation to account for turbulence-induced distortions for both uplink and downlink. Simulations under vary ing system dimensions, weather conditions, and zenith angles demonstrate that HD-BB84 achieves higher key rates, superior noise tolerance, and more favorable probability distributions of the key rate compared to HD-Extended B92, highlighting the advantages of high-dimensional encoding for robust satellite-based QKD.
commentary: This comprehensive thesis tackles one of quantum cryptography's biggest practical challenges: making quantum key distribution work reliably across the vast distances that only satellites can bridge. While ground-based quantum networks are limited to a few hundred kilometers due to fiber losses, satellite-based QKD promises truly global quantum-secure communications by beaming quantum states through space. The research's detailed modeling of atmospheric effects like turbulence and pointing errors addresses real-world engineering hurdles that have plagued early satellite QKD demonstrations, potentially accelerating the timeline for operational quantum communication networks. This work becomes increasingly critical as organizations worldwide race to deploy quantum-safe communications before large-scale quantum computers arrive to break today's encryption standards.

title: The Transformation-Response Framework: An Operational Reformulation of Quantum Mechanics
summary: We present the transformation-response framework, an operational reformulation of quantum mechanics. A quantum state is not a Hilbert space object but the catalog of a system's responses to all physical transformations: for each operation $g$ from the system's local group $G$, an interference experiment gives a complex value $χ(g)$. The collection $\{χ(g): g\in G \}$ is the characteristic function and defines the state. The only postulate is that $χ$ is positive-definite, encoding the requirement that no superposition of transformations yields negative probability. From this single assumption, the entire standard formalism is derived: Hilbert space via GNS construction, Born rule via Bochner theorem, Schrödinger equation from group automorphisms, and especially Feynman path integral as a Trotter limit. The framework is background-independent and time-neutral: time is a coordinate along a one-parameter subgroup of $G$. It also reveals a new physical constraint, product order positivity, which may lead to testable predictions. The framework provides a unified, economical, and falsifiable foundation for quantum theory rooted in operational primitives.
commentary: This arXiv paper presents a bold attempt to rebuild quantum mechanics from the ground up using only operational measurements and group theory, potentially offering the most minimalist foundation for quantum theory to date. The transformation-response framework is particularly intriguing because it derives all the familiar quantum formalism—including the Schrödinger equation and Feynman path integrals—from a single postulate about positive-definite response functions, while remaining agnostic about the underlying nature of time and space. What makes this approach especially compelling is its introduction of "product order positivity," a new mathematical constraint that could lead to experimentally testable predictions, giving physicists a way to probe whether this reformulation captures something deeper about quantum reality. While highly theoretical, this kind of foundational work has historically led to practical breakthroughs—quantum computing itself emerged from similar deep questions about the mathematical structure of quantum mechanics.

title: Quantum Mechanical Studies of Photodissociation Dynamics on Quantum Computers
summary: Theoretical quantum dynamics calculations scale deeply with system size, rendering classical calculations intractable for complex systems. While quantum computing offers a natural solution, its application to nuclear quantum dynamics remains scarce. Here, we present a quantum algorithm to study photodissociation dynamics on quantum computers, benchmarked on the NOCl molecule. The wavefunction is propagated via a split-operator method, utilizing the Quantum Fourier Transform and unitary transformation matrix to switch representations. To impose outgoing boundary conditions on a truncated grid, we use a non-unitary absorbing potential propagator, implemented through a dilation scheme. The photodissociation cross section is calculated from the auto-correlation function, which is extracted using the Hadamard test. Our quantum computing results agree well with benchmarks under ideal conditions, and we further demonstrate that the algorithm is robust to noise and statistical sampling errors, indicating the promising application of noisy devices to quantum dynamics studies.
commentary: This article represents a significant step toward using quantum computers for real-world chemistry problems, specifically demonstrating how quantum algorithms can simulate molecular photodissociation dynamics - the process where molecules break apart when hit by light. The researchers successfully implemented their algorithm on the NOCl molecule, showing that quantum computers can handle the complex quantum mechanical calculations needed to understand how chemical bonds break, which classical computers struggle with for larger systems. What's particularly encouraging is their demonstration that the algorithm remains robust even with the noise and errors present in today's quantum devices, suggesting this approach could be practical on near-term quantum computers. This work opens the door for quantum computers to eventually tackle larger, more complex molecular systems that are completely beyond classical simulation capabilities, potentially revolutionizing computational chemistry and our understanding of photochemical processes.

title: Impact of gate-voltage noise on silicon spin-qubit variational quantum eigensolvers
summary: Quantum computers offer a route to outperform classical methods in tasks such as molecular simulation, motivating hybrid algorithms like the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) for near-term devices. Silicon spin qubits are a promising platform for scalable quantum computation, but their performance is limited by hardware imperfections -- most notably charge-noise-induced potential fluctuations and static miscalibration of gate-electrode voltages -- which degrade quantum gate fidelities and, ultimately, algorithmic accuracy. Here we develop a hardware-algorithm co-simulation framework for silicon quantum-dot processors that links 3D electrostatics to effective $g$-factors and exchange couplings, and propagates voltage-level noise through realistic control pulses. Using VQE for $\mathrm{H}_2$ ground-state energy estimation as a circuit-level testbed, we study both static scaling/offset errors on the gate-electrode voltages and stochastic fluctuations modeled as random-telegraph noise with tunable amplitudes and switching times. At the gate level, we show that exchange-based two-qubit gates are roughly an order of magnitude more sensitive to these types of noise than ESR-driven single-qubit rotations. Quantum process tomography and Kraus-operator analysis further distinguish coherent and incoherent contributions and quantify the fraction of error that is, in principle, correctable by a compensating unitary. Embedding these noise models into the VQE circuit, we identify regimes of miscalibration strength and noise switching time compatible with chemically accurate energy estimates, and discuss how statistical post-processing based on the full distribution of noisy energy estimates could further improve accuracy.
commentary: This research tackles a critical challenge for silicon spin qubits by developing the first comprehensive simulation framework that connects real-world voltage noise all the way through to algorithmic performance in quantum chemistry applications. The findings reveal that two-qubit exchange gates are about ten times more vulnerable to charge noise than single-qubit operations, providing crucial guidance for hardware designers working to scale up silicon quantum processors. By using the Variational Quantum Eigensolver as a testbed, the authors bridge the gap between low-level hardware imperfections and high-level algorithm accuracy, offering a roadmap for co-optimizing silicon qubit control systems and quantum algorithms. This work is particularly timely as silicon spin qubits emerge as strong contenders for large-scale quantum computers, since understanding and mitigating charge noise will be essential for achieving quantum advantage in practical applications.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Fast Operator Selection in Adaptive VQE
summary: Adaptive variational quantum algorithms like ADAPT-VQE construct tailored ansätze by iteratively selecting operators from a pool using gradient-based criteria. While this avoids oversized parameter spaces, repeatedly scanning the full pool incurs a classical cost that scales linearly with pool size-a major bottleneck for systems with long-range interactions or large operator sets. Here, we reformulate adaptive operator selection as a graph-based decision problem and introduce a graph neural network (GNN) policy that predicts the next entangling operator directly from the interaction graph and state-dependent observables. Training data are generated from exact simulations of disordered long-range spin chains, using gradient magnitudes as supervision signals. The learned policy accurately reproduces the dominant structure of the greedy gradient-based selection rule, significantly outperforming heuristics based solely on interaction strength. Integrated into a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) workflow, this GNN-VQE approach achieves energy errors close to standard ADAPT-VQE while drastically reducing full-pool gradient evaluations. To test transferability beyond spin models, we evaluate the policy on small active-space molecular benchmarks (LiH and BeH_$2$). We find the GNN is highly effective as a shortlist generator: exact rescoring over just a few GNN-proposed candidates recovers near-oracle rollout behavior while searching only a small fraction of the pool. These results demonstrate that adaptive circuit construction contains learnable structure that can be exploited to accelerate variational quantum algorithms.
commentary: This research tackles one of the most computationally expensive bottlenecks in adaptive variational quantum algorithms - the need to evaluate gradients across entire operator pools at each iteration, which becomes prohibitively costly for complex quantum systems. By reformulating operator selection as a graph learning problem, the authors developed a neural network that can predict which quantum operators to add next based on the system's interaction structure and current quantum state, dramatically reducing the classical overhead that often dominates these hybrid algorithms. The approach shows promising transferability from spin systems to molecular problems, suggesting it could accelerate quantum chemistry simulations where ADAPT-VQE has shown great promise but suffered from scalability issues. This work represents a compelling fusion of classical machine learning and quantum algorithm design that could make adaptive quantum algorithms practical for larger, more realistic quantum systems.

title: Randomized simulation of quantum channels using small ancilla
summary: We study the problem of implementing a quantum channel using a small ancilla with classical randomization and postselection on an output failure flag. The simulation is probabilistic, but exact conditioned on success. We prove that any unital channel on a $d$-dimensional system can be simulated with ancilla dimension $k$ and success probability $Ω(\frac{k}{\log d})$. Equivalently, every unital channel on $n$ qubits can be simulated with constant success probability using only $O(\log n)$ ancillary qubits. We show that this tradeoff is best possible by constructing a family of channels which cannot be simulated with success probability better than $O(\frac{k}{\log d})$. We also show that the class of \textit{highly noncommutative} channels, which includes random channels, admits constant-success simulation with just a single ancillary qubit. We further show that this model of simulation necessarily fails for strongly non-unital channels and discuss possible extensions involving adaptivity. On the technical side we rely on a partition-based protocol and matrix concentration inequalities, including the recent refinement of noncommutative Khintchine inequalities due to Bandeira, Boedihardjo and van Handel.
commentary: This breakthrough demonstrates a fundamental quantum computing principle: you can efficiently simulate complex quantum operations using surprisingly few extra qubits, as long as you're willing to accept some probability of failure. The researchers proved that any unital quantum channel (operations that preserve certain quantum properties) can be simulated with only logarithmic overhead in ancilla qubits while maintaining constant success probability—a massive improvement over naive approaches that might require exponential resources. This work has profound implications for quantum algorithm design and error correction, potentially enabling more efficient implementations of quantum protocols when perfect deterministic execution isn't required. The mathematical framework also reveals deep connections between quantum channel structure and simulation complexity, opening new avenues for understanding what makes certain quantum operations fundamentally harder to implement than others.

Detailed in Nature Physics, the experiment investigates a hardware interface designed to address the data-loading bottleneck that occurs when [...] The post Experimental Implementation of a Bucket-Brigade QRAM Architecture on a Superconducting Processor appeared first on Quantum Computing Report .

The Zhejiang University team's work in Nature Physics tackles the fundamental challenge that quantum algorithms requiring large datasets face, where data preparation can consume exponential time and negate quantum advantages. While early-stage, this hardware implementation moves QRAM from theoretical concept to physical reality, potentially unlocking practical applications for quantum machine learning and database search algorithms that have long been limited by data input constraints. The research demonstrates how circuit-based approaches can begin addressing the scalability challenges that will be essential for quantum computers to process real-world datasets effectively.

title: Scientists identify the origin of noise in spin qubit quantum processors
summary: A spin qubit, in which quantum information is encoded in the spin state of an electron, is one of the most promising platforms for quantum computing. Spin qubits exhibit long coherence times and are compatible with advanced semiconductor manufacturing technologies. The leading implementation of spin qubits involves confined electrons inside quantum dots, a nanoscale semiconductor architecture that behaves like a controllable artificial atom. Recent advances have enabled high-fidelity operation of single- and two-qubit gates, exceeding the threshold required for certain surface code quantum error correction techniques.
commentary: This research represents a crucial step toward practical quantum computers by pinpointing the sources of decoherence that plague spin qubit systems, which are among the most promising candidates for large-scale quantum processors due to their compatibility with existing semiconductor fabrication. Understanding and controlling noise is absolutely essential for quantum error correction to work effectively, as even the most sophisticated error correction codes can only handle errors below certain thresholds. The fact that spin qubits are now achieving fidelities that exceed requirements for surface code implementation is particularly exciting, as this puts them in serious contention with other leading qubit technologies like superconducting circuits. By identifying specific noise mechanisms, researchers can now engineer targeted solutions to push spin qubit performance even further, potentially accelerating the timeline for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Ferroelectrical Switching as a Probe of Quantum Damping in Magnetic Spin Systems
summary: While damped spin dynamics is important for the understanding of magnetic materials, clear signatures of \emph{quantum corrections} to the Gilbert damping mechanism remain elusive. We propose a route to distinguish quantum and classical Gilbert spin damping using ferroelectric control of a magnetic dimer. Ab initio calculations for dimers on ferroelectric substrates show that polarization reversal switches the inter-spin exchange between ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic regimes. We formulate a magnetization-based diagnostic that relates magnetization traces to entanglement dynamics, which enables ferroelectrical on/off control of dimer entanglement. Material-informed quantum Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert simulations illustrate how the signature of magnetization dynamics can, in principle, be used to infer the existence of quantum Gilbert spin damping. This minimal and non-volatile platform connects first-principles modeling to experimentally accessible observables and provides a starting point for voltage-controlled quantum entanglement in magnetic spin networks.
commentary: This research tackles a fundamental challenge in quantum magnetism by proposing an elegant experimental method to detect quantum effects in magnetic damping, which have remained frustratingly difficult to observe despite decades of theoretical predictions. The team's approach using ferroelectric substrates to electrically switch magnetic interactions between ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic states offers a practical pathway to control and measure quantum entanglement in magnetic systems. What makes this particularly exciting is the connection between readily observable magnetization dynamics and the underlying quantum entanglement, potentially opening the door to voltage-controlled quantum devices based on magnetic materials. This work bridges the gap between fundamental quantum many-body physics and practical quantum technologies, offering a new platform for exploring quantum effects in condensed matter systems.

title: Coherent versus stochastic error injection on a repetition-code logical qubit in superconducting hardware
summary: The performance of quantum error correction (QEC) codes is limited by the underlying physical noise. Theoretical studies show that coherent and stochastic noise have different effects when performing QEC with either surface or repetition codes. We use the bitflip repetition code, realized in a transmon quantum processor, as a testbed to experimentally study the impact of injecting coherent versus stochastic errors on the logical performance. We adapt a scalable free-fermion simulator to simulate the experiments and we modify a subset sampling technique to efficiently sample stochastic noise in the quantum circuit. In the experiment, we do not observe the difference in logical fidelity predicted by simulation for either the distance-3 or distance-5 repetition codes. We hypothesize that this discrepancy could be explained by small drifts in qubit frequencies, which introduce phase-coherent noise that `stochastifies' the injected coherent errors. Our work contributes to advancing an understanding of how coherent errors affect experimental QEC.
commentary: This research tackles a crucial real-world challenge in quantum error correction: the gap between theoretical predictions and experimental reality when dealing with different types of noise. While theory suggests that coherent errors (which maintain quantum phase relationships) should behave very differently from random stochastic errors in repetition codes, the IBM team found no such difference in their superconducting quantum processor experiments. The suspected culprit is frequency drift in the qubits themselves, which appears to scramble coherent errors into effectively random ones, highlighting how subtle hardware imperfections can dramatically alter error correction performance. This work underscores the importance of bridging theory and practice in quantum error correction, showing that even small, seemingly innocuous effects like qubit drift can reshape how errors propagate through quantum circuits.

title: Suppression of Quasiparticle Poisoning to $10^{-11}$ Levels in Superconducting Qubits via Infrared Shielding
summary: Quasiparticle poisoning bottlenecks superconducting qubits, limiting coherence and the scalability of quantum processors. In this work, we systematically investigate quasiparticle poisoning in superconducting qubits under three infrared (IR) shielding configurations, ranging from a dedicated multi-layer design to a simplified implementation. By measuring quasiparticle-induced parity switching, we demonstrate a suppression of the switching rate by over four orders of magnitude via the implementation of improved shielding. In the best configuration, the rate decreases over time following cooldown and reaches 0.069$\,$Hz on day 34, corresponding to an anticipated quasiparticle density per Cooper pair of $1.88\times10^{-11}$. To our knowledge, this represents the lowest quasiparticle density reported in the literature to date. The remaining quasiparticle population is likely dominated by sporadic phonon bursts stemming from mechanical stress release in the on-chip films, as well as from the surrounding environment. The effective qubit temperature follows the phonon bath down to 17$\,$mK, enabling initialization errors of $\sim 0.01\%$ for 3$\,$GHz qubits. These results demonstrate that proper IR shielding and thermalization are essential for suppressing quasiparticle poisoning and enabling high-coherence, scalable superconducting qubit systems.
commentary: This breakthrough tackles one of the most persistent challenges in superconducting quantum computing: quasiparticle poisoning, where unwanted energy excitations corrupt qubit states and destroy quantum information. By implementing sophisticated infrared shielding, the researchers achieved a staggering four-order-of-magnitude reduction in quasiparticle density to just 1.88×10^-11 per Cooper pair - the lowest ever reported - essentially creating an ultra-clean quantum environment where qubits can maintain coherence far longer. The work demonstrates that with proper engineering of the electromagnetic environment around quantum processors, initialization errors can be reduced to just 0.01%, a critical milestone for building the large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers that major tech companies are racing to develop. This represents a significant step toward solving the scalability problem that has long plagued superconducting quantum systems, showing that environmental control may be just as important as the qubits themselves.

title: Experimental Demonstration of Free-Space Unidimensional Continuous-Variable Quantum Key Distribution Under High Detector Noise
summary: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD), which uses quadratures of the electromagnetic field, enables practical quantum communication using standard telecommunication technologies. Unidimensional CV-QKD (UD-CVQKD) simplifies the implementation by restricting modulation to a single quadrature. In this work, we experimentally demonstrate a free-space Gaussian-modulated UD-CVQKD system operating under a high detector electronic-noise regime (1.4 shot-noise units). The system employs polarized coherent states with signal and local oscillator co-propagating in the same spatial mode in orthogonal polarizations, ensuring stable interference. System security is analyzed under both untrusted (UTD) and trusted (TD) detector noise models. While no positive secret key rate is obtained under the UTD model, the TD model enables secure key generation over a finite range of modulation variances, highlighting the critical role of detector trust in high-noise conditions. A maximum secret key rate of 270 kbps is achieved at an optimal modulation variance of 11.57. Furthermore, secure operation requires high-transmittance (low-loss) channels under such noise conditions. This study demonstrates the practical feasibility of free-space UD-CVQKD in realistic high electronic-noise detection constraints and highlights detector electronic noise as a key limiting factor in practical systems.
commentary: This experimental work tackles one of the most stubborn practical challenges in quantum cryptography: making continuous-variable quantum key distribution work reliably in free-space environments where detector noise typically kills the quantum advantage. The researchers achieved a respectable 270 kbps secure key rate using a simplified unidimensional approach that requires only standard telecom equipment, making quantum-secured communications more accessible than complex discrete-variable systems. However, the stark difference between trusted and untrusted detector noise models reveals a critical vulnerability - the system only works when you can guarantee your detectors haven't been tampered with, which significantly limits real-world deployment scenarios. This study provides valuable insights for the quantum communication community about the fundamental trade-offs between system simplicity, noise tolerance, and security assumptions in practical quantum cryptography implementations.

title: Projector Quantum Variational Ansatz
summary: Quantum computing offers several algorithms to compute the ground state of a problem Hamiltonian. The most desirable algorithms belong to the Fault Tolerant QuantumComputing (FTQC) regime, such as quantum algorithms with repetitive structure like Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) and Quantum Signal Processing (QSP). However, in the Noisy In-termediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) regime, the most realistic approaches involve Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) algorithms and their variants. VQE is an algorithm that searches for a parametrized unitary matrix called an ansatz whose purposeis to transform an easily prepared initial state into the groundstate of a given Hamiltonian. Adaptive Derivative-AssembledPseudo-Trotter (ADAPT)-VQE is a variant of VQE that im-proves this approach by constructing the ansatz iteratively so that the associated quantum circuit is as shallow as possible. A major difference between FTQC (i.e. not variational) algorithms and VQE is that FTQC algorithms do not construct a state transitiondirectly. Instead, they construct a projector that identifies the ground state using ancillary qubits that flag the good solution. The desired state is then obtained via amplitude amplification orpost-selection. In this work, we propose a VQE ansatz whose structure is more similar to that of an FTQC algorithm. Depending on its parametrization, this ansatz can be equivalent to either an Intermediate Scale Quantum (ISQ)-QSP or to an ADAPT-VQE quantum circuit structure. Our experimental results show that this first proposal of Projector Variational Ansatz (PVA) converges with a shallower ansatz than the usual ADAPT-VQE.
commentary: This research bridges a crucial gap between near-term NISQ algorithms and future fault-tolerant quantum computing by developing a variational ansatz that mimics the projector-based approach used in powerful FTQC algorithms like Quantum Phase Estimation. The work is particularly significant because it offers a potential pathway to access some benefits of fault-tolerant algorithms within current noisy quantum hardware limitations, while maintaining the shallow circuit depths that ADAPT-VQE provides. By creating a hybrid approach that can switch between ISQ-QSP and ADAPT-VQE structures depending on parametrization, this could help quantum computing researchers better prepare for the eventual transition from NISQ to fault-tolerant systems. This represents an important step toward making quantum algorithms more robust and scalable across different hardware generations.

title: Quantum correlations and coherence in a two-qubit anisotropic $XY$ under magnetic field
summary: We study thermal quantum correlations and coherence in Heisenberg $XY$ model with anisotropic interactions under a uniform magnetic field $ B $. Using concurrence $C$, local quantum uncertainty (LQU), Bell-Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) nonlocality $ \mathbb{B}$, and coherence $C_l$ as quantifiers, we analyze how magnetic anisotropy $ δ_m $, coupling anisotropy $ δ_c $, Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction $ D $, temperature $ T $, and magnetic field $ B $ modulate quantum resources. At low temperatures and relevant magnetic fields, the entanglement is maximized, but exhibits sudden death for $ δ_m = 0 $, which turns into a smooth decay as $ δ_m $ increases, highlighting its stabilizing role. LQU shows that stronger anisotropy suppresses quantum correlations, while $ \mathbb{B} $ induces a non-monotonic response peaking at a critical field $ B_c $. Bell-CHSH nonlocality violations ($ \mathbb{B} > 2 $) persist below $ B_c $, but thermal noise ($ T \geq 1 $) suppresses them. Coherence $ C_l $ is most robust to thermal fluctuations, especially for high \( δ_m \), which also dampens abrupt quantum phase transitions. The DM interaction is essential for entanglement generation, with $ D $ and anisotropy synergistically enhancing correlation resilience. We identify a hierarchy of thermal degradation: nonlocality ($ \mathbb{B} $) vanishes first, followed by entanglement ($ C $), then general quantum correlations (LQU), while coherence $ C_l $ persists the longest. These results demonstrate tunable control of quantum resources via anisotropy and external parameters, providing insights for the design of robust spin-based quantum technologies.
commentary: This theoretical study provides crucial insights for quantum hardware designers by mapping out exactly how different types of quantum correlations degrade under realistic conditions like temperature fluctuations and magnetic field variations. The research reveals a fascinating hierarchy where quantum coherence proves most resilient to thermal noise, outlasting even entanglement - a finding that could guide the development of more robust quantum processors that leverage coherence-based protocols. Particularly valuable is the identification of how magnetic anisotropy can prevent the abrupt "sudden death" of entanglement, instead allowing for smoother degradation that might be easier to manage in practical quantum systems. These results offer a theoretical roadmap for optimizing qubit designs and operating conditions to maximize quantum advantage in noisy, real-world environments.

title: Exact noise characterization of entanglement distribution in star networks
summary: Multipartite entanglement forms the core of many networking applications. In the near-term future, it is expected that multipartite distribution will be achieved first through star topologies, making it important to understand the noise incurred during the distribution process. In such networks, elementary links are created stochastically and successful links must be stored while waiting for the remaining links, causing memory decoherence that depends on the random waiting times. We derive analytical expressions for both the average noise and its distribution, when distributing GHZ states under memory dephasing in star networks. We study and compare two distribution protocols: the factory and piecemaker protocol. Furthermore, we find expressions for the case of a global cut-off (allowing fast optimization of the cut-off without requiring Monte Carlo simulations) and extend the analysis for the factory protocol to depolarizing noise for arbitrary states.
commentary: This research tackles one of the most pressing practical challenges in quantum networking: understanding exactly how noise accumulates when distributing multipartite entangled states across star-shaped networks, which are expected to be the first scalable quantum network architectures. The work provides crucial analytical tools that allow network designers to optimize protocols without expensive simulations, addressing the fundamental problem that quantum memories decohere while waiting for all network links to be established successfully. By comparing factory and piecemaker distribution protocols and deriving exact noise characterizations, this study offers essential insights for building real-world quantum networks where timing uncertainties and memory limitations are unavoidable constraints. The mathematical framework developed here could significantly accelerate the development of practical quantum communication networks by enabling precise performance predictions and protocol optimization.

title: Solution of the Equation-of-Motion Phonon Method eigenvalue problems on the D-Wave quantum annealer
summary: The solution of large-scale eigenvalue problems is crucial in nuclear many-body theory, where Hamiltonian matrices often reach extremely large dimensions. Quantum computing opens new perspectives for addressing such demanding problems. Although the Quantum Phase Estimation algorithm offers, in principle, a systematic route to matrix diagonalization, its practical deployment demands levels of coherence and error correction that current quantum hardware cannot yet support. A viable near-term strategy is instead to exploit quantum annealing, which enables the recasting of eigenvalue problems into quadratic unconstrained binary optimization formulations that can be addressed by existing annealing-based processors. Here, we propose a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm that combines quantum annealing and classical deflation to iteratively extract the full eigenspectrum of both standard and generalized eigenvalue problems. We benchmark this method on eigenvalue problems arising from the Equation of Motion Phonon Method performing calculations on real quantum hardware. Our approach illustrates the capabilities and limitations of near-term quantum devices in addressing nuclear eigenvalue problems.
commentary: This research demonstrates a clever workaround for one of quantum computing's most promising but currently impractical applications - solving the massive eigenvalue problems that arise in nuclear physics simulations. While the theoretically optimal Quantum Phase Estimation algorithm remains out of reach for today's noisy quantum hardware, these researchers successfully adapted D-Wave's quantum annealer to tackle real nuclear many-body calculations by reformulating eigenvalue problems as optimization tasks. The hybrid approach, which combines quantum annealing with classical deflation techniques to extract complete eigenspectra, represents exactly the kind of near-term quantum advantage we need to see - taking quantum hardware as it exists today and finding meaningful scientific applications. This work could open doors for quantum-assisted materials science and nuclear engineering calculations well before fault-tolerant quantum computers become available.

title: Nonreciprocal optomechanical entanglement in an asymmetric Fabry-Perot cavity
summary: Nonreciprocal transmission (classical nonreciprocity) in optomechanical systems based on asymmetric Fabry-Perot (F-P) cavities has been theoretically proposed and experimentally demonstrated. However, nonreciprocal quantum effects, particularly nonreciprocal quantum entanglement, remain unexplored in such systems. Here, we propose to generate nonreciprocal optomechanical entanglement in an asymmetric F-P cavity and discuss the connection between the nonreciprocal transmission and nonreciprocal quantum entanglement. We reproduce the nonreciprocal transmission spectra by solving the quantum Langevin equations, and then discuss the optimal parameters to achieve nonreciprocal optomechanical entanglement in the system. We show that a greater and more robust optomechanical entanglement can be approached in the asymmetric F-P cavities, in comparing with the symmetric cavities. Furthermore, we find that the degrees of classical and quantum nonreciprocities do not exhibit positive correlation as expected. Our work shows that the classical and quantum nonreciprocities can be realized simultaneously in the asymmetric F-P cavities, which provide a platform to explore the connection between classical and quantum nonreciprocities.
commentary: This research breaks new ground by demonstrating that asymmetric Fabry-Perot cavities can generate nonreciprocal quantum entanglement, where quantum correlations behave differently depending on direction - a quantum analog of how certain materials allow light to pass through more easily in one direction than the other. What makes this particularly intriguing is the surprising finding that classical nonreciprocity (directional transmission) and quantum nonreciprocity (directional entanglement) don't necessarily correlate as one might expect, suggesting these phenomena operate through fundamentally different mechanisms. The enhanced robustness of entanglement in asymmetric cavities compared to symmetric ones could prove valuable for quantum sensing and communication applications, where maintaining quantum correlations in noisy environments remains a major challenge. This work opens up a new research direction at the intersection of quantum optics and mechanical systems, potentially leading to novel quantum devices that exploit directional quantum effects.

title: Scalable Quantum Algorithms for Gutzwiller Projection
summary: Quantum simulation requires highly accurate input states. Gutzwiller-projected Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) states provide physically motivated input states for solving strongly correlated lattice models, but their preparation on a quantum computer is hindered by the non-trivial nature of the Gutzwiller projection. We construct scalable quantum algorithms for this task by combining a circuit construction for arbitrary BCS states with the amplitude amplification for Gutzwiller projection (AAGP) procedure. AAGP yields a quadratic reduction in the number of projection queries compared with measurement-based postselection and leads to substantially improved fault-tolerant resource scaling. For projected BCS states optimized for the square-lattice $t$-$J$ model, we find that the projected-state weight decreases exponentially with system size, but the quadratic improvement is still large enough at physically relevant finite sizes to make a decisive practical difference. In particular, for a 100-site benchmark, AAGP reduces the required number of projection queries by about seven orders of magnitude. These results establish AAGP as an enabling input-state preparation protocol for projected BCS states in quantum simulation.
commentary: This research tackles a critical bottleneck in quantum simulation by developing a dramatically more efficient way to prepare Gutzwiller-projected BCS states, which are essential starting points for studying strongly correlated quantum materials like high-temperature superconductors. The amplitude amplification technique delivers a quadratic speedup over traditional measurement-based approaches, translating to a staggering seven-orders-of-magnitude reduction in computational overhead for realistic 100-site systems. While the projected-state weights still decrease exponentially with system size, this algorithmic breakthrough makes previously intractable quantum simulations of complex materials feasible on near-term fault-tolerant quantum computers. The work represents a significant step toward using quantum computers to solve some of condensed matter physics' most challenging problems, particularly in understanding exotic phases of matter where classical methods fall short.

title: A superconducting surface-code processor with lattice-surgery logical operations
summary: Fault-tolerant logical operations are fundamental for scalable quantum computation. Here, we report the experimental realization of lattice-surgery operations between a pair of distance-three surface-code logical qubits on a planar superconducting processor. During repeated syndrome extraction cycles, the logical qubits exhibit per-cycle error rates of $0.0365(2)$ and $0.0282(1)$, respectively, after leakage events are rejected. By leveraging joint initialization and lattice splitting, we deterministically prepare a logical Bell state, confirming genuine bipartite entanglement via the error-corrected logical state fidelity. We further execute a two-qubit Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm at the logical level to demonstrate algorithmic utility in a fault-tolerant framework. Finally, to achieve universal control, we implement magic-state injection and gate teleportation to realize continuous non-Clifford rotations about the logical $X$ axis. For the logical $R_{X}(π/4)$ gate, we achieve a logical gate fidelity of $0.943_{-9}^{+10}$ conditioned on the absence of detected errors. These results establish lattice surgery as a practical and versatile paradigm for logical computation in near-term surface-code architectures, representing a critical milestone toward scalable fault-tolerant quantum advantage in superconducting circuits.
commentary: This breakthrough demonstrates the first practical implementation of lattice surgery operations between surface-code logical qubits, marking a pivotal step toward truly scalable quantum computation. The team not only achieved fault-tolerant logical operations with impressive error rates below 4% per cycle, but also executed a complete quantum algorithm (Deutsch-Jozsa) entirely at the logical level using error-corrected qubits. Most significantly, they implemented magic-state injection to perform non-Clifford gates, which are essential for universal quantum computation but notoriously difficult to achieve fault-tolerantly. This work bridges the gap between theoretical surface code proposals and practical quantum processors, offering a clear roadmap for building large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computers using existing superconducting technology.

title: Demystifying Objectivity with Operator Algebra Quantum Error Correction
summary: Quantum Darwinism extends the decoherence formalism to explain how classicality and objectivity emerge from quantum mechanics. However, existing approaches often capture only partial aspects of objectivity, leading to its mischaracterization and making it difficult to pin down precisely. By connecting quantum Darwinism to operator algebra quantum error correction, we show that the emergence of objectivity can be identified with the algebraic local recoverability of quantum codes. Applying this algebraic framework to stabilizer codes, we show that it yields a far more precise characterization of classicality and redundancy, unifies the traditional measures of objectivity, enables efficient classification via coding-theoretic tools, and supports large-scale Clifford simulations of decoherence dynamics.
commentary: This article bridges two major quantum computing concepts - quantum error correction and quantum Darwinism - to provide a more rigorous mathematical foundation for understanding how classical information emerges from quantum systems. The key insight is connecting the abstract notion of "objectivity" in quantum Darwinism to the concrete algebraic structure of quantum error correction codes, particularly stabilizer codes that are widely used in quantum computing. This connection not only clarifies long-standing conceptual puzzles about the quantum-to-classical transition but also opens up practical computational tools for simulating how quantum information becomes classical through decoherence. The work could prove valuable for both fundamental quantum theory and practical quantum error correction schemes, as it provides coding-theoretic methods to analyze and classify different types of quantum-to-classical transitions.

title: Fun with Graph States: Nonlocal Bell Pairs and the Arf Invariant
summary: We study inner products and partial amplitudes of graph states--a commonly employed class of quantum states, which are specified by graphs. We find that the magnitudes of these quantities are simply related to the rank of the adjacency matrix of the graph over F_2 while the phase is determined by the Arf invariant of its quadratic refinement. These facts motivate a nonlocal tensor factorization of the Hilbert space, with respect to which all graph states are products of Bell pairs with unentangled ancillae. These results may illuminate the quantum advantage in the framework of Measurement-Based Quantum Computation and suggest that graph states can be usefully visualized in the language of algebraic topology. In addition, we develop a specialized technique for computing expectation values of qubit-wise permutations in graph states, which is useful for calculating multi-invariants.
commentary: This research unveils a surprisingly elegant mathematical structure underlying graph states, revealing that these widely-used quantum states can be decomposed into collections of nonlocal Bell pairs paired with unentangled ancillary qubits. The discovery that graph state properties are governed by fundamental algebraic concepts like the Arf invariant and adjacency matrix rank over finite fields provides new theoretical tools for understanding why measurement-based quantum computation works so effectively. This mathematical insight could lead to more efficient ways to prepare and manipulate graph states in quantum hardware, potentially streamlining protocols for quantum sensing and distributed quantum computing where graph states serve as essential resources. The work bridges quantum information theory with algebraic topology in a way that may unlock new perspectives on quantum advantage and inspire novel quantum algorithms.

title: Breakeven demonstration of quantum low-density parity-check codes
summary: High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes are a leading candidate for fault-tolerant quantum computing. They feature higher encoding rates than planar alternatives such as the surface code, but their implementation often entails significant hardware hurdles like the need for long-range couplers. We leverage the flexibility of a trapped-ion quantum computer to demonstrate nine quantum error-correcting codes with starkly different qubit connectivity requirements on a single device without any hardware reconfiguration. These experiments span three families of quantum error-correcting codes: qLDPC codes, topological codes, and concatenated codes. With a qLDPC code encoding 4 logical qubits into 18 physical qubits, we achieve a logical error rate up to $9\times$ better than a previous demonstration of a similar code on superconducting solid-state qubits. Moreover, our implementation exhibits breakeven performance, with some instances achieving qubit lifetimes comparable to or slightly exceeding that of our trapped-ion qubits. We use a novel implementation of the optical-metastable-ground (OMG) architecture for addressable mid-circuit measurement and reset, which enables us to perform these experiments without any ion transport or dedicated coolant ions, requirements that typically consume a large fraction of the runtime or ion count of trapped-ion quantum computers.
commentary: This research marks a crucial milestone in quantum error correction by demonstrating breakeven performance with quantum low-density parity-check codes, where logical qubits actually live as long as the underlying physical qubits - a key threshold for practical quantum computing. The team's achievement of encoding 4 logical qubits into just 18 physical qubits while maintaining error rates 9 times better than previous demonstrations shows the promise of qLDPC codes as more efficient alternatives to the widely-studied surface code. What makes this particularly impressive is the use of trapped-ion hardware's inherent flexibility to test nine different error correction schemes on the same device, proving these codes can work without exotic hardware modifications like long-range couplers that other platforms might require. The novel OMG architecture implementation that eliminates the need for ion shuttling could significantly streamline future trapped-ion quantum computers while making sophisticated error correction more practical.

title: Nanostructure modelling with early fault tolerant quantum computers
summary: Semiconductor nanostructures are central to many developing technologies. Notably, double quantum dots are especially important for semiconductor spin-qubit architectures, quantum sensing applications, and quantum-dot solar cells. Accurate modelling is highly desirable but conventional methods can struggle when dynamics involve more than two interacting electrons. In this work, we present a quantum simulation framework capable of addressing multi-electron double quantum dots. We adopt an efficiently scaling 1$^\text{st}$ quantised representation of the system and develop algorithms based on both Trotterisation and qubitisation. Incorporating insights from classical simulations enables us to produce resource estimates that are more realistic than those obtained from theoretical error bounds. Using a standard surface code model with physical noise at $10^{-3}$, our results indicate that the ground-state energy of four electrons in a double quantum dot can be estimated in approximately 24 hours using 226k physical qubits, or an eight-electron system in 3.4 days with 314k qubits (with runtimes falling dramatically when more qubits are available). We anticipate that incorporating very recent advances including dense surface code architectures (Low et al. arXiv:2605.30455) may reduce these costs significantly further. We conclude that early fault tolerant computers may prove to be valuable tools for designing mature-era quantum technologies.
commentary: This research presents a compelling chicken-and-egg scenario where near-term fault-tolerant quantum computers could accelerate the development of better quantum hardware by simulating the complex multi-electron dynamics in quantum dots that are too difficult for classical computers to handle accurately. The authors provide realistic resource estimates showing that meaningful simulations of 4-8 electron systems could run on quantum computers with hundreds of thousands of physical qubits within reasonable timeframes, making this a prime candidate for early quantum advantage applications. What makes this particularly exciting is that improved understanding of quantum dot behavior could directly feed back into better spin-qubit designs and quantum sensing devices, creating a virtuous cycle where quantum computers help design their own next generation. The practical focus on semiconductor nanostructures also bridges quantum computing with established semiconductor manufacturing, potentially accelerating commercial quantum technology development.

title: Semidefinite-programming hierarchies for classically simulable state families
summary: Identifying whether a state family admits an irreducible quantum advantage is a fundamental task in quantum resource theory and quantum information processing. Here we study classically simulable state families, namely those residing within the convex hull of pairwise commuting families and therefore admitting a classical explanation. We develop a complete semidefinite-programming (SDP) hierarchy characterizing the set of classically simulable state families in arbitrary finite dimension. The key step is to reformulate classical simulability as a feasibility problem over deterministic response functions and auxiliary positive-operator-valued measures (POVMs) simulable by rank-one projective measurements. We establish a complete SDP hierarchy for rank-one projectively simulable POVMs and transfer the resulting characterization to state families, yielding both primal feasibility tests and dual affine witnesses certifying failure of classical simulability. Applying the hierarchy to state families mixed with depolarizing noise gives computable upper bounds on the critical classical visibility, which are matched by explicit classical simulations in several symmetric examples. These results provide a systematic convex-optimization framework for certifying classical simulability of quantum state families.
commentary: This work tackles one of quantum computing's most fundamental questions: when do quantum states actually provide an advantage over classical systems, and when are they just classical phenomena in disguise? The researchers developed a systematic mathematical framework using semidefinite programming to determine whether families of quantum states can be simulated classically, providing both computational tools to test for genuine quantum advantage and methods to find the optimal classical simulations when they exist. This is particularly valuable for understanding the boundary between quantum and classical resources in noisy quantum devices, where decoherence can wash out quantum advantages and leave systems that appear quantum but are actually classically simulable. The framework could help quantum algorithm designers identify when their protocols retain genuine quantum benefits despite noise, and guide experimentalists in determining the noise thresholds beyond which their quantum devices lose their computational edge.

title: Deployed trusted-node quantum key distribution over 300 km with a multi-core fiber access link
summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) is increasingly considered for deployment in realistic communication networks, where long distances, heterogeneous fiber infrastructure, and coexistence with classical traffic present substantial challenges. Here, we demonstrate trusted-node QKD between Linköping University and the Stockholm hub of the Swedish national quantum communication infrastructure over 270 km of deployed single-mode fiber, extended by a 33 km multi-core fiber (MCF) segment emulating a metropolitan access link, for a total distance of 303 km. The two sub-links use commercial QKD systems whose receivers are interfaced with external superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors, enabling operation at losses beyond those supported by standard internal gated-mode detectors. We operate the link while actively switching the QKD channel between two MCF cores, with co-propagating Ethernet traffic and injected broadband optical noise in the other cores. The results demonstrate the integration of commercial QKD into demanding, dynamically reconfigurable fiber infrastructure relevant to future hybrid quantum-classical networks. Finally, using the generated secret keys, we illustrate how limited and time-varying QKD throughput affects one-time-pad-protected image transmission: image fidelity depends strongly on the available QKD-generated key budget and the choice of compression algorithm, highlighting application-level challenges for QKD-based encryption in realistic scenarios.
commentary: This demonstration represents a significant step toward practical quantum key distribution deployment by successfully operating QKD systems over Sweden's actual telecommunications infrastructure spanning 303 kilometers, including multi-core fiber segments that will be crucial for future quantum-classical hybrid networks. The researchers tackled real-world challenges by showing QKD can coexist with classical Ethernet traffic, handle dynamic channel switching between fiber cores, and operate through the high losses encountered in deployed fiber networks using advanced superconducting detectors. Perhaps most importantly, the team went beyond just proving the technology works to examine how limited QKD key generation rates affect actual encrypted communications, revealing that image transmission quality depends heavily on available key budgets and compression choices. This kind of end-to-end analysis of QKD performance in realistic network conditions provides invaluable insights for organizations planning quantum-secured communications infrastructure.

title: Barbell Codes: qLDPC Codes for Superconducting Quantum Hardware
summary: The major challenge on the way to fault-tolerant quantum computing comes from the insufficient quality of hardware components and the difficulty of scaling their number without further compromising fidelity. Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check (qLDPC) codes offer a promising solution by encoding logical qubits with low overhead and at a comparatively high code distance. However, it remains an open question how to scalably implement efficient qLDPC codes on fixed-connectivity quantum chips without increasing hardware complexity to enable the non-local interactions in their underlying QEC cycles. We resolve this challenge for the first time by introducing a family of qLDPC "barbell" codes accompanied by a realistic chip layout that natively supports all required two-qubit interactions. Crucially, the hardware complexity required to implement barbell codes remains constant as code distance increases. We provide a detailed investigation into the feasibility of all required hardware components and simulate a specific family of barbell codes against circuit-level noise. We find that, with a modest overhead of $<30$ data qubits per logical qubit, barbell codes can preserve information at a physical noise strength of $10^{-4}$ for several trillion QEC cycles. Simulations of logical multi-Pauli measurements, performed with circuits tailored to the chip, yield similar logical performance per QEC round, indicating that entangling gates between logical qubits in barbell codes can be realized fault-tolerantly.
commentary: This research tackles one of the most pressing challenges in quantum error correction by introducing "barbell" qLDPC codes that can be efficiently implemented on real superconducting quantum hardware without requiring exotic connectivity patterns. The breakthrough lies in designing both the error correction code and the chip layout together, ensuring that all necessary qubit interactions can be performed natively on a 2D grid while maintaining constant hardware complexity as the system scales up. With simulations showing these codes can protect quantum information for trillions of error correction cycles using fewer than 30 physical qubits per logical qubit at realistic noise levels, this work provides a concrete pathway toward fault-tolerant quantum computing on near-term hardware. The practical focus on implementability rather than just theoretical performance marks a crucial step from laboratory concepts toward deployable quantum error correction systems.

title: Quantum computing for accurate large-scale electronic-structure calculations: DFT-embedded, post-processed quantum-selected configuration interaction
summary: We present a multilevel embedding framework for quantum chemistry calculations on a quantum computer. In our framework, a quantum algorithm treats the strongly correlated active space, while a high-level wave-function method such as coupled cluster theory or multireference perturbation theory recovers the remaining correlation in the surrounding region. A sampling-based quantum algorithm, quantum-selected configuration interaction, bridges the quantum and classical treatments. The entire calculation is embedded in a low-cost density functional theory description of the surrounding environment using Manby's projection technique. We apply the framework to organic, metal-organic, and metallic systems, computing bond dissociation energies, adsorption energies, and reaction barriers using only the subset of qubits of a 144-qubit superconducting quantum computer at the University of Osaka and achieving $\sim$1 kcal/mol agreement with classical references for a Menshutkin $\mathrm{S_N2}$ reaction inside a carbon nanotube. Our results may open the way to quantitatively reliable quantum-classical hybrid calculations for large-scale chemical systems.
commentary: This research represents a major step toward making quantum computers practically useful for chemistry by cleverly combining quantum and classical methods in a layered approach. The team's multilevel embedding framework uses quantum algorithms only where they're most needed - for the trickiest electron correlations - while relying on established classical methods for the bulk of the calculation, maximizing efficiency on today's limited quantum hardware. Achieving 1 kcal/mol accuracy for chemical reactions using just a subset of a 144-qubit system demonstrates that meaningful quantum advantage for real-world chemistry problems may be closer than expected. This hybrid approach could be the key to unlocking quantum computing's potential for drug discovery, materials design, and catalysis long before we have fault-tolerant quantum computers.

title: Rapid Gaussian Boson Sampling Circuit Screening for GKP States Creation via a Two-Stage Machine Learning Surrogate
summary: Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states are essential non-Gaussian resources for fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing, enabling logical qubit encoding with intrinsic robustness against errors. Several approaches to GKP state preparation have been explored, including measurement-based protocols in circuit QED and trapped-ion systems, cat-state breeding, and photon-subtraction schemes. However, these methods are either restricted to specific platforms or require deep non-Gaussian resource chains with exponentially low success probabilities. Gaussian Boson Sampling (GBS) offers a compelling all-photonic alternative by generating non-Gaussian states through measurement-induced nonlinearity, without the need for matter-based ancilla or active feedforward. Nevertheless, its practical implementation is limited by the exponential computational cost of evaluating matrix hafnians-#P-complete functions that govern photon-number probabilities. To address this challenge, we introduce a two-stage Histogram Gradient Boosting surrogate pipeline that predicts, without any hafnian computation, the optimal heralding pattern, circuit fidelity, and post-selection probability for candidate GBS circuits, while reserving exact quantum simulation exclusively for surrogate-selected candidates. Trained on circuit configurations across 3-5 optical modes, the surrogate achieves 90.0% GKP-detection accuracy on a held-out set, representing a 23.7 percentage-point improvement over the baseline, with a fidelity mean absolute error of 0.032 and a log-scale post-selection probability $R^2 = 0.837$, reducing the total simulation burden by approximately 90%.
commentary: This article tackles one of quantum computing's most pressing challenges: creating the exotic quantum states needed for fault-tolerant computation without breaking the bank computationally. GKP states are like the Swiss Army knife of photonic quantum computing - they can encode logical qubits while naturally protecting against certain errors - but generating them through Gaussian Boson Sampling requires calculating mathematical functions so complex they're in the "#P-complete" category of computational nightmares. The researchers' clever solution uses machine learning as a fast screening tool to identify promising quantum circuits before running the expensive exact calculations, achieving 90% accuracy while dramatically reducing computational overhead. This approach could accelerate the development of practical photonic quantum computers by making it feasible to explore the vast space of possible quantum circuits for generating these crucial resource states.

title: Shattering the Symmetry Trap in Fixed-Ansatz VQE: An Accelerated ADAPT-VQE Study of Three Pillar Molecules under Bravyi-Kitaev Mapping
summary: Fixed-ansatz Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VQE), such as the Unitary Coupled Cluster with Singles and Doubles (UCCSD) framework, frequently suffer from severe initialization paralyzation and zero-gradient traps when evaluated using the non-local Bravyi-Kitaev (BK) fermion-to-qubit mapping. In this work, we systematically demonstrate how the Adaptive Derivative-Assembled Pseudo-Trotter (ADAPT-VQE) framework shatters these structural limitations across three distinct electronic and geometric molecular pillars: Lithium Hydride ($\text{LiH}$), Hydrogen Fluoride ($\text{HF}$), and Water ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$), under heavily stretched or asymmetric multi-reference configurations. While conventional UCCSD-VQE flatlines completely at a zero energy shift ($0.000000$~Ha) due to global phase cancellations inherent to the BK tree structures, our dynamic ADAPT-VQE loop successfully isolates the dominant symmetry-breaking operators using analytical commutator gradients. To bypass the severe $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$ computational bottlenecks of dense matrix exponentiation and Singular Value Decomposition on larger registers, we implement a highly optimized, vector-based Taylor series expansion state-evolution engine. Our numerical results show that the accelerated ADAPT-VQE framework achieves instant, exact Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) convergence within the very first macro-cycle across all three molecular systems, maintaining absolute numerical stability up to a 12-qubit register space. This study establishes a robust, hardware-efficient path for simulating strongly correlated, highly polarized triatomic chemical environments on near-term local architectures.
commentary: This article tackles a critical roadblock in quantum chemistry simulations where traditional VQE algorithms get stuck in "symmetry traps" that prevent them from finding correct molecular ground states, particularly when using the Bravyi-Kitaev qubit mapping scheme. The researchers demonstrate that ADAPT-VQE can dynamically break through these limitations by adaptively selecting the most important quantum operators, achieving exact solutions for key test molecules like water and lithium hydride where fixed approaches completely fail. What makes this especially significant is their development of an accelerated computational engine that bypasses the typical scaling bottlenecks, potentially making these more sophisticated VQE variants practical for near-term quantum hardware. This work represents an important step toward making quantum computers genuinely useful for molecular simulation by solving fundamental algorithmic challenges that have limited previous approaches.

C12's proprietary approach could potentially unlock scalable manufacturing of carbon nanotube quantum processors, offering an alternative pathway to the silicon and superconducting qubit platforms that currently dominate the industry. This development represents the kind of foundational engineering advance that often precedes major leaps in quantum computing capability and commercialization.

title: No-go theorems on simulating uncertainty principle's signatures
summary: Uncertainty principle, one of the most iconic features of quantum mechanics, was originally viewed as a fundamental limitation. Since the inception of quantum information science, researchers began to use it to achieve quantum advantages. To better understand the origin of these advantages, an essential question is: To what extent can the uncertainty principle's signatures be simulated by a single measurement? As a single measurement clearly cannot demonstrate the uncertainty principle, such a simulation, if exists, implies the claimed advantages may either stem from other quantum features, or just be reproducible in a less resourceful way. In this work, we report a series of noise-robust no-go theorems, showing that strong enough signatures of uncertainty principle cannot be simulated by a single measurement, even when assisted by quantum pre- or post-processing. This signature is modelled by complementary instruments. We completely characterise complementary instruments by a numerically feasible measure and show that they are necessary and sufficient resources for the advantage in an operational task that aims to unambiguously send classical information.
commentary: This work provides crucial theoretical foundations for understanding when quantum advantages are truly "quantum" by proving that strong signatures of the uncertainty principle cannot be faked with classical single measurements, even with quantum preprocessing. The research addresses a fundamental question in quantum information science: whether the advantages we attribute to quantum uncertainty might actually be achievable through simpler, less resource-intensive methods. By establishing these "no-go theorems," the authors help validate that certain quantum sensing and communication protocols genuinely require the unique properties of quantum mechanics, rather than just clever classical tricks. This kind of theoretical grounding is essential for the field as it moves toward practical applications, ensuring that claimed quantum advantages represent real computational or sensing benefits worth the engineering complexity of quantum systems.

title: Symmetry-adapted qubit encoding with complete active space and Bravyi--Kitaev mapping for quantum chemistry on a quantum computer
summary: We present a symmetry-adapted qubit encoding with complete active space (SAE-CAS) for quantum chemistry on fault-tolerant and near-term quantum processors. Building on exact-symmetry encodings, we extend symmetry-adapted mappings to approximate $Z$-symmetries corresponding to frozen-core and virtual orbitals, thereby reducing qubit requirements without significant loss of accuracy. We derive the mapping from the second-quantised Hamiltonian to active-space qubit Hamiltonians, prove its equivalence to the canonical CAS Hamiltonian with frozen-core and virtual-orbital projection, and integrate it with point-group and spin-parity symmetry encodings via affine Clifford transformations to maximise qubit reduction while preserving the target symmetry sector. The same framework also accommodates the Bravyi--Kitaev mapping, yielding an SAE-CAS-BK variant that is unitarily equivalent to SAE-CAS. Numerical benchmarking on nine small molecules using UCCSD and a hardware-efficient shifted-circular-alternating (HE-SCA) ansatz shows that SAE-CAS reduces qubit counts and Pauli-operator weight, yields shallower circuits with fewer parameters, and often accelerates VQE convergence; with HE-SCA it consistently reaches CAS reference energies in cases where JW-CAS does not converge within the tested budgets. We provide an open-source implementation in the Python package QuantumSymmetry. SAE-CAS offers a route to resource-efficient molecular simulations on fault-tolerant and near-term quantum processors.
commentary: This article tackles one of quantum computing's most promising applications—molecular simulation—by introducing a clever encoding scheme that dramatically reduces the number of qubits needed without sacrificing accuracy. The SAE-CAS method exploits molecular symmetries to compress quantum chemistry problems into smaller, more manageable forms, potentially making complex molecular simulations feasible on near-term quantum devices that have limited qubit counts. What makes this particularly exciting is that the researchers demonstrate their approach not only uses fewer qubits but also creates shallower quantum circuits that converge faster, addressing multiple bottlenecks that currently limit quantum advantage in chemistry. With an open-source implementation already available, this could accelerate the timeline for quantum computers to tackle real-world drug discovery and materials science problems.
